\section{The integral counts and the relative deficit}
\label{sec:counts}

Let $X_m$ be the complex nine-dimensional manifold constructed in
Proposition~\ref{geo:family}, and let $Y$ be the surface of
Proposition~\ref{dyn:surface}. Set
\[
 C_m=X_m\times\CP^1,\qquad M_m=X_m\times Y.
\]
Both products are simply connected and Kähler, of real dimensions $20$
and $22$. Our task is to compare the ordinary Morse count on $C_m$ with
the stable Morse count on $M_m$. By Theorem~\ref{morse:equality}, this
amounts to computing their quantities $\lambda$.

\subsection{The two torsion profiles}
The ranks in Lemma~\ref{geo:surfaces} give $b(S_2)=b(S_3)=8$.
Since $\CP^1\times\CP^1$ has free homology of ranks $(1,2,1)$ in degrees
$(0,2,4)$, the center $Z_3=S_3\times\CP^1\times\CP^1$ has
$b(Z_3)=32$. The integral blow-up decomposition in
\eqref{geo:family-homology} therefore yields
\begin{equation}\label{counts:rank-X}
 b(X_m)=10+m(6\cdot8+4\cdot32)=10+176m.
\end{equation}

All the homology shifts in that decomposition are even. Torsion in the
surface degrees $1$ and $2$ consequently gives two separate lists, in
degrees $1+2j$ and $2+2j$. For either list we have
\begin{equation}\label{counts:base-profiles}
 \Tor H_{1+2j}(X_m;\Z)\cong\Tor H_{2+2j}(X_m;\Z)
 \cong(\Z/2)^{ma_j}\oplus(\Z/3)^{mq_j},
\end{equation}
where the finite sequences, indexed starting at $j=1$, are
\[
 a=(2,2,2,2,2,2),\qquad q=(1,3,4,4,3,1),
\]
and all other entries are zero. To see the second sequence directly, let
$u$ record a shift by two homological degrees. The product with
$\CP^1\times\CP^1$ and the four blow-up shifts give
\[
 (u+u^2+u^3+u^4)(1+2u+u^2)
 =u+3u^2+4u^3+4u^4+3u^5+u^6.
\]
The first sequence records six blow-up shifts of two copies of $\Z/2$.
Equation~\eqref{counts:base-profiles} accounts for all torsion.

For nonnegative integers $a,q$, the primary-generator identity
\eqref{morse:primary-maximum} gives
\begin{equation}\label{counts:generator-maximum}
 d\bigl((\Z/2)^a\oplus(\Z/3)^q\bigr)=\max(a,q).
\end{equation}
In particular, generator counts must be computed in each degree
before summing over degrees.

If a factor $B$ has torsion-free homology concentrated in even degrees, put
$e_k=\rank H_{2k}(B;\Z)$ for $k\geq0$. The integral Künneth theorem replaces $a$ and $q$
by their convolutions with $e$:
\[
 (e*a)_j=\sum_{k\geq0}e_k a_{j-k},\qquad
 (e*q)_j=\sum_{k\geq0}e_k q_{j-k}.
\]
There are no additional Künneth torsion terms. For $C_m$ use $e=(1,1)$;
for $M_m$, \eqref{dyn:Y-homology} gives $e=(1,6,1)$. The resulting
profiles in either degree list, divided by $m$, are shown in
Table~\ref{tab:profiles}.

\begin{table}[tb]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llr@{}}
\toprule
Product and primary part & Multiplicities in one degree list & Sum\\
\midrule
$C_m$, $2$-primary & $(2,4,4,4,4,4,2)$ & $24$\\
$C_m$, $3$-primary & $(1,4,7,8,7,4,1)$ & $32$\\
$C_m$, generators & $(2,4,7,8,7,4,2)$ & $34$\\
\midrule
$M_m$, $2$-primary & $(2,14,16,16,16,16,14,2)$ & $96$\\
$M_m$, $3$-primary & $(1,9,23,31,31,23,9,1)$ & $128$\\
$M_m$, generators & $(2,14,23,31,31,23,14,2)$ & $140$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Primary torsion multiplicities and their entrywise maxima.
Every displayed entry is multiplied by $m$, and the same list occurs
once in odd degrees and once in even degrees. The generator row takes
the maximum within each column, as in
\eqref{counts:generator-maximum}.}
\label{tab:profiles}
\end{table}

It follows that
\begin{align}
 \sum_i t_i(C_m)&=2\cdot34m=68m,&
 \sum_i t_i(M_m)&=2\cdot140m=280m.\label{counts:torsion-totals}
\end{align}
The free ranks are $b(C_m)=2b(X_m)$ and $b(M_m)=8b(X_m)$, so
\begin{equation}\label{counts:lambda}
 \lambda(C_m)=20+488m,\qquad
 \lambda(M_m)=80+1968m.
\end{equation}
The table also explains the sign of the gap. The total multiplicity at
each individual prime is four times as large for $M_m$ as for $C_m$.
However, relative to the $3$-primary row, taking the degreewise maximum
adds $2m$ generators per parity for $C_m$ and $12m$ for $M_m$. Thus the
generator count for $M_m$ exceeds four times that for $C_m$ by
$(12-4\cdot2)m=4m$ per parity. The free-rank contributions cancel,
and the two parities and the factor $2$ in $\lambda$ give
\begin{equation}\label{counts:gap}
 \lambda(M_m)-4\lambda(C_m)
 =2(280-4\cdot68)m=16m.
\end{equation}

\subsection{Completion of the construction}
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}]
Fix $m\geq1$. Choose any Kähler form on $X_m$ and equip
$M_m=X_m\times Y$ with its product with the invariant form on $Y$ from
Proposition~\ref{dyn:surface}. Theorem~\ref{morse:equality} applies to
$C_m$ and $M_m$, since both are closed and simply connected and their
real dimensions are at least $9$. It supplies an ordinary Morse function
$h_m$ on $C_m$ with $20+488m$ critical points, and it gives
$\SM(M_m)=80+1968m$.

Corollary~\ref{dyn:product}, applied to $X_m$ and $h_m$, produces a smooth
one-periodic Hamiltonian $H_m$ on $M_m$ with precisely
\[
 4\#\Crit(h_m)=80+1952m
\]
fixed points. They are all nondegenerate. Simple connectivity of $M_m$
makes every corresponding loop along $\phi_{H_m}^t$ contractible, so the
two fixed-point counts agree.

Finally,
\[
 \frac{\SM(M_m)-\#\Fix(\phi_{H_m}^1)}{\SM(M_m)}
 =\frac{16m}{80+1968m}
 =\frac{m}{5+123m}\geq\frac1{128},
\]
where the inequality is equivalent to $m\geq1$.
For a given $R>0$, take
$m=\max\{1,\lceil(R-80)/1968\rceil\}$. Then
$\SM(M_m)\geq R$, while the dimension and $\delta=1/128$ remain fixed.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{counts:field-bounds}
The total Betti numbers of $M_m$ over fields of characteristic $2$ and $3$
are respectively $80+1792m$ and $80+1920m$. Indeed, the universal coefficient
theorem adds twice the total primary multiplicity to the integral free
rank, and Table~\ref{tab:profiles} gives those multiplicities. Both
numbers are smaller than the fixed-point count $80+1952m$. Over any
field of characteristic different from $2$ and $3$, the total Betti
number is $80+1408m$. Thus taking a single
coefficient field does not recover the integral generator count used here:
the prime contributing the larger number of generators changes with the
degree.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}\label{counts:integral-Floer-bound}
The integral Floer bound of Bai--Xu uses homology graded modulo twice the
minimal Chern number~\cite[Theorem~A]{BaiXu2022}; see also
\cite[Corollary~1.2]{BaiXu2026}. The minimal Chern number $N$ is the positive generator of
the nonzero subgroup $c_1(TM_m)(\pi_2(M_m))\subset\Z$.
For $M_m$ it is $1$: if $E\subset Y$ is an exceptional line, then its
tangent bundle has degree $2$ and its normal bundle has degree $-1$.
Thus $c_1(TM_m)$ evaluates to $1$ on the sphere $\{x\}\times E\subset M_m$.
In the grading modulo $2$, all odd-degree groups are combined and all
even-degree groups are combined. In either parity, Table~\ref{tab:profiles}
then gives primary torsion multiplicities $96m$ and $128m$. The minimum
number of torsion generators is therefore $128m$ in each parity. The
cyclically graded integral bound is
\[
 b(M_m)+2(128m+128m)=80+1920m,
\]
which is smaller than the fixed-point count by $32m$. The strict gap in
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} relies on keeping the integer homological degrees
separate when computing the stable Morse number.
\end{remark}

\section{From Morse functions to Hamiltonian fixed points}
\label{dyn:section}
\label{sec:dynamics}

The dynamical construction turns a Morse function on
$X\times\CP^1$ into a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism of $X\times Y$ with
four times as many fixed points.  Here $Y$ will be a K\"ahler surface
with a Hamiltonian involution whose fixed locus consists of four
projective lines.  We give the construction of
\cite[Section~4]{OpenAICompanion}, including the argument that counts
all fixed points and checks their nondegeneracy in the ambient manifold.

We use the convention
\[
  \omega(X_f,\,\cdot\,)=df
\]
for the Hamiltonian vector field of a smooth function $f$.  A fixed
point $x$ of a diffeomorphism $\Phi$ is nondegenerate when
$d_x\Phi-I$ is invertible.  The following elementary estimate will
exclude additional fixed points after a small autonomous perturbation.
It is of the same type as Yorke's lower bound on periods for Lipschitz
vector fields~\cite{Yorke1969}; only a positive lower bound is needed here.

\begin{lemma}[A lower bound on nonconstant periods]
\label{dyn:short-period}
Let $V$ be a smooth vector field on a closed smooth manifold $P$, with
flow $\psi^s$.  There is a number $\tau>0$ such that
\[
  0<T<\tau,\qquad \psi^T(x)=x
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad V(x)=0.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose finitely many coordinate balls covering $P$, each with closure
contained in a larger coordinate ball in the same chart.  Bounds on
the coordinate speeds, together with the positive distances from
the smaller closed balls to the boundaries of the larger balls, give
$\eta>0$ such that a trajectory starting in a smaller ball stays in
its larger ball for time $\eta$.  Choose a common positive Lipschitz
constant $L$ for the coordinate expressions of $V$ on the larger
balls; their coordinate images are convex and their closures may be
taken compact in the charts.

Suppose $\psi^T(x)=x$ with $0<T<\eta$.  In a chart containing the whole
trajectory, write its coordinates as $y:[0,T]\to\R^d$, and write $v$
for the coordinate vector field.  Put
\[
  m=\max_{0\leq t\leq T}|v(y(t))|,
\]
and choose $t_0$ where the maximum is attained.  Since $y(T)=y(0)$,
\[
  \int_0^T v(y(t))\,dt=0,
  \qquad |y(t)-y(t_0)|\leq Tm.
\]
Consequently
\[
\begin{split}
  m
  &=\left|\frac1T\int_0^T
       \bigl(v(y(t_0))-v(y(t))\bigr)\,dt\right|\\
  &\leq\frac{L}{T}\int_0^T |y(t_0)-y(t)|\,dt
   \leq LTm.
\end{split}
\]
For $T<\tau:=\min\{\eta,1/L\}$ this forces $m=0$, proving the claim.
\end{proof}

The next proposition applies the estimate to an involution.  Its
fixed components are symplectic submanifolds.  An invariant extension
of Morse functions on those components supplies the perturbation;
squaring the perturbed map will identify every one of its fixed points.

\begin{proposition}[Perturbing a Hamiltonian involution]
\label{dyn:involution}
Let $(P,\omega)$ be a closed symplectic manifold and let $g:P\to P$
be a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism with $g^2=\mathrm{id}_P$.  Write
$\Fix(g)=F_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup F_r$ for its connected fixed
components.  For each $j$, let $h_j:F_j\to\R$ be a smooth Morse
function.  There is a smooth $g$-invariant function $f:P\to\R$
restricting to $h_j$ on $F_j$ such that, for all sufficiently small
$\epsilon>0$, its Hamiltonian flow $\psi^s$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
\label{dyn:fixed-set}
  \Fix(\psi^\epsilon\circ g)
    =\bigsqcup_{j=1}^r\Crit(h_j).
\end{equation}
Every fixed point in this equality is nondegenerate.  Moreover,
$\psi^\epsilon\circ g$ is the time-one map of a smooth one-periodic
Hamiltonian.  If $P$ is simply connected, all fixed-point loops along
the resulting Hamiltonian path are contractible.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Average a Riemannian metric over $\{\mathrm{id}_P,g\}$.  At a fixed
point $x$, the resulting exponential chart intertwines $g$ with
$d_xg$.  Thus the fixed locus is locally a smooth submanifold,
whose tangent space at $x$ is
\[
  E_x^+=\ker(d_xg-I).
\]
This local description and compactness imply that it has finitely
many connected components, each a smooth closed submanifold.
The involution gives the
decomposition
\[
  T_xP=E_x^+\oplus E_x^- ,
  \qquad E_x^-=\ker(d_xg+I).
\]
For $u\in E_x^+$ and $v\in E_x^-$, symplecticity gives
\[
  \omega_x(u,v)
  =\omega_x(d_xg(u),d_xg(v))=-\omega_x(u,v).
\]
Thus the summands are symplectically orthogonal.  Since $\omega_x$
is nondegenerate, its restriction to each summand is nondegenerate
as well.  In particular, $F_j$ is symplectic and $E_x^-$ is its
symplectic normal space.

Using disjoint tubular neighborhoods of the $F_j$ and smooth cutoff
functions, extend the $h_j$ to a smooth function $\widetilde f$ on $P$.
Set
\[
  f=\tfrac12(\widetilde f+\widetilde f\circ g).
\]
This function is $g$-invariant and restricts to $h_j$ on $F_j$.
Invariance and symplecticity imply $g_*X_f=X_f$, so $g$ commutes with
$\psi^s$.  At a point $x\in F_j$, invariance also implies
$d_xf(v)=0$ for $v\in E_x^-$.  Orthogonality of the two summands then
shows that $X_f$ is tangent to $F_j$, where it is the Hamiltonian
vector field of $h_j$ for $\omega|_{F_j}$.  Hence
\begin{equation}
\label{dyn:equilibria}
  x\in F_j:\qquad X_f(x)=0
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d_xh_j=0.
\end{equation}

Put $\Phi_\epsilon=\psi^\epsilon\circ g$.  The commutation relation
and $g^2=\mathrm{id}_P$ give
\[
  \Phi_\epsilon^2=\psi^{2\epsilon}.
\]
Let $\tau$ be given by Lemma~\ref{dyn:short-period} for $X_f$, and
take $2\epsilon<\tau$.  Any fixed point $x$ of $\Phi_\epsilon$
satisfies $\psi^{2\epsilon}(x)=x$, so the lemma gives $X_f(x)=0$.
The flow therefore fixes $x$ at every time, and
$\psi^\epsilon(g(x))=x$ implies $g(x)=x$.  Equation~\eqref{dyn:equilibria}
now places $x$ among the prescribed critical points.  Conversely,
each prescribed critical point is fixed by both $g$ and $\psi^\epsilon$.
This proves~\eqref{dyn:fixed-set}.

We next check nondegeneracy in both the tangent and the normal
directions.  At a point $x$ in the finite set~\eqref{dyn:fixed-set},
let $A_x=d_xX_f$ be the linearization at the equilibrium.  Then
\[
  d_x\psi^\epsilon=\exp(\epsilon A_x).
\]
Equivariance implies that $A_x$ commutes with $d_xg$, so it preserves
$E_x^+$ and $E_x^-$.  Denote its restrictions by $A_x^+$ and $A_x^-$.
On $E_x^+=T_xF_j$, differentiating the Hamiltonian equation at the
critical point gives
\[
  \omega_x(A_x^+u,v)=\operatorname{Hess}_x h_j(u,v).
\]
The Morse condition therefore makes $A_x^+$ invertible.  Since
\[
  \frac{\exp(\epsilon A_x^+)-I}{\epsilon}
       \longrightarrow A_x^+
       \quad\text{as }\epsilon\longrightarrow0,
\]
the tangent block of $d_x\Phi_\epsilon-I$ is invertible for all
sufficiently small positive $\epsilon$.  The normal block is
\[
  -\exp(\epsilon A_x^-)-I\longrightarrow-2I,
\]
and is likewise invertible.  There are finitely many prescribed
critical points, so a single positive upper bound for $\epsilon$
ensures nondegeneracy at all of them as well as the fixed-set equality.

Finally, choose a smooth Hamiltonian $K_s$, $0\leq s\leq1$, whose
time-one map is $g$.  Choose nonnegative smooth functions $a,b$ with
integral one and supports contained in two successive disjoint
subintervals of $(0,1)$.  Define
\[
  A(t)=\int_0^t a(u)\,du,\qquad
  H_\epsilon(t,x)=a(t)K_{A(t)}(x)+\epsilon b(t)f(x),
  \qquad 0\leq t\leq1.
\]
During the support of $a$, the flow traverses the path of $K_s$ from
the identity to $g$.  During the later support of $b$, it follows
the flow of $f$ for total time $\epsilon$.  Thus its time-one map
is $\psi^\epsilon\circ g$.  Since $H_\epsilon$ vanishes near both
endpoints of $[0,1]$, its periodic extension is smooth.  If $P$ is
simply connected, every fixed-point loop of this specified path is
contractible.
\end{proof}

We now construct the surface that gives four copies of the Morse
problem.  Blowing up each isolated fixed point of a half-turn
replaces it by a fixed projective line.

\begin{proposition}[The surface with four fixed curves]
\label{dyn:surface}
Let $Y$ be the complex blow-up of $\CP^1\times\CP^1$ at
\[
  \{0,\infty\}\times\{0,\infty\}.
\]
There is a circle-invariant K\"ahler form $\omega_Y$ for which the
lifted diagonal circle action is Hamiltonian.  Its half-turn $g_Y$
has fixed locus precisely the four exceptional curves
$E_1,\ldots,E_4$, each isomorphic to $\CP^1$.  Along these curves,
$d g_Y$ is the identity on the tangent bundle and minus the identity
on the symplectic normal bundle.  Moreover, $Y$ is simply connected
and its integral homology is
\begin{equation}
\label{dyn:Y-homology}
  H_i(Y;\Z)\cong
  \begin{cases}
    \Z,&i=0,4,\\
    \Z^6,&i=2,\\
    0,&\text{otherwise}.
  \end{cases}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
In affine coordinates, the diagonal circle action on
$\CP^1\times\CP^1$ is
\[
  t\cdot(z,w)=(e^{2\pi it}z,e^{2\pi it}w),
  \qquad t\in\R/\Z.
\]
It preserves the four centers and therefore lifts holomorphically
to $Y$.  Proposition~\ref{geo:blowup} shows that $Y$ is K\"ahler and
simply connected.  Average a K\"ahler form over the lifted circle
action to obtain an invariant K\"ahler form $\omega_Y$.  If $V$ is
the infinitesimal generator, Cartan's formula gives
\[
  d\bigl(\omega_Y(V,\,\cdot\,)\bigr)
     =\mathcal L_V\omega_Y=0.
\]
As $H^1(Y;\R)=0$, there is a smooth function $k:Y\to\R$ with
$dk=\omega_Y(V,\,\cdot\,)$.  Thus $V=X_k$, and the autonomous
Hamiltonian $k/2$ has time-one map $g_Y$.

The downstairs half-turn fixes exactly the four centers.  Using
the coordinate $z$ near $0$ and $1/z$ near $\infty$ in each factor,
the circle weights at the centers are
\[
  (1,1),\quad(1,-1),\quad(-1,1),\quad(-1,-1).
\]
For weights $(\alpha,\beta)$ the induced action on the exceptional
line is
\[
  [z_1:z_2]\longmapsto
  [e^{2\pi i\alpha t}z_1:e^{2\pi i\beta t}z_2].
\]
When the signs differ this action has nonzero relative weight
$\beta-\alpha=\pm2$; in all four cases its value at $t=1/2$ is the
identity.  To see the action also in the normal direction, use the
local blow-up model
\[
  \{(\ell,v):\ell\in\CP^1,\ v\in\ell\subset\C^2\}.
\]
The downstairs half-turn is $v\mapsto-v$, so its lift is
\[
  (\ell,v)\longmapsto(\ell,-v).
\]
It fixes exactly the zero section, with derivative $+I$ on its
tangent space and $-I$ on its normal line.  The symplectic normal
space is the negative eigenspace by the orthogonality argument in
Proposition~\ref{dyn:involution}.  Away from the exceptional curves,
the blow-down is an equivariant isomorphism.  There are therefore
no additional fixed points.

Finally, each point blown up has complex codimension two, so
\eqref{geo:blowup-homology} adds one free generator in degree two.
The integral homology of $\CP^1\times\CP^1$ is free with ranks
$(1,2,1)$ in degrees $(0,2,4)$, respectively.  Four blow-ups give
\eqref{dyn:Y-homology}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Product realization]
\label{dyn:product}
Let $X$ be a connected closed simply connected K\"ahler manifold,
let $\omega_X$ be any K\"ahler form on $X$, and let $(Y,\omega_Y)$ be as in
Proposition~\ref{dyn:surface}.  Give $M=X\times Y$ the product form
$\omega_X\oplus\omega_Y$ and put $C=X\times\CP^1$.
For every smooth Morse function $h:C\to\R$, there is a smooth
one-periodic Hamiltonian $H$ on $M$ whose time-one map has only
nondegenerate fixed points and satisfies
\begin{equation}
\label{dyn:product-count}
  \#\Fix(\phi_H^1)
   =\#\Fix_0(\phi_H^1;H)
   =4\,\#\Crit(h).
\end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The pullback to $M$ of $k/2$ generates the Hamiltonian involution
$g=\mathrm{id}_X\times g_Y$ for the given product form.  Its fixed
components are exactly $X\times E_1,\ldots,X\times E_4$.  Choose
isomorphisms $E_j\cong\CP^1$ and use them to pull $h$ back to Morse
functions $h_j$ on these four components.  Each $h_j$ has
$\#\Crit(h)$ critical points.  Proposition~\ref{dyn:involution}
applies to their induced symplectic forms and produces exactly
the fixed points counted in~\eqref{dyn:product-count}, all
nondegenerate.  Finally, $M$ is simply connected, so every
fixed-point loop for the constructed path is contractible.
\end{proof}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

The fixed-point problem for Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms compares
symplectic dynamics with the topology measured by Morse functions.
Here we distinguish two integral homological counts: one retains every
integer degree, while the other retains only parity. Torsion at different
primes makes these counts genuinely different. We construct a
Hamiltonian diffeomorphism attaining the parity count on a manifold
whose geometric stable Morse number is strictly larger.

For a closed smooth manifold $W$, put
\[
 b(W)=\sum_i\rank H_i(W;\Z).
\]
For a finite abelian group $G$, let $d(G)$ be its minimum number of
generators, with $d(0)=0$. Define
\begin{align}
 \lambda(W)&=b(W)+2\sum_i d\bigl(\Tor H_i(W;\Z)\bigr),
 \label{eq:lambda}\\
 \overline H_{\bar i}(W;\Z)&=
       \bigoplus_{k\equiv i\pmod 2}H_k(W;\Z),\nonumber\\
 \beta_{\Z}^{\mathrm{cyc}}(W)&=b(W)+
       2\sum_{\bar i\in\Z/2}
       d\bigl(\Tor\overline H_{\bar i}(W;\Z)\bigr).
 \label{eq:cyclic}
\end{align}
The first expression is degreewise; in the second, torsion summands
may be combined across all degrees of the same parity.
For example, $d(\Z/2\oplus\Z/3)=1$, whereas placing these two
groups in distinct degrees of the same parity contributes $2$ to the
degreewise sum but only $1$ to the paritywise sum.
Consequently $\beta_{\Z}^{\mathrm{cyc}}(W)\leq\lambda(W)$,
and strictness is possible.

We use the geometric convention for the stable Morse number:
$\SM(W)$ is the minimum number of critical points of a Morse function
on $W\times\R^k$, for some integer $k\geq0$, which equals a
nondegenerate quadratic form in the auxiliary variables outside a
compact set. For $k=0$ this includes ordinary Morse functions on $W$.
Write $\Morse(W)$ for the minimum number of critical points of an
ordinary Morse function on $W$.

For a smooth Hamiltonian $H:(\R/\Z)\times M\to\R$ on a closed
symplectic manifold $(M,\omega)$, we use the convention
$\omega(X_{H_t},\cdot)=dH_t$ and write $\phi_H^t$ for its flow
starting at the identity. A fixed point $x$ of $\phi_H^1$ is
nondegenerate if $D\phi_H^1(x)$ has no eigenvalue $1$.
Let $\Fix_0(\phi_H^1;H)$ denote the fixed points for which
$t\mapsto\phi_H^t(x)$ is contractible in $M$.

\begin{theorem}
\label{thm:main}
There exist a simply connected closed K\"ahler manifold $(M,\omega)$
of complex dimension $1666$ and a smooth one-periodic Hamiltonian $H$
such that
\[
 c_1(TM)(\pi_2(M))=\Z,
\]
every fixed point of $\phi_H^1$ is nondegenerate, and
\begin{align*}
 \#\Fix(\phi_H^1)
 &=\#\Fix_0(\phi_H^1;H)
  =\beta_{\Z}^{\mathrm{cyc}}(M)=1\,872\,232,\\
 \SM(M)&=\beta_{\Z}^{\mathrm{cyc}}(M)+32=1\,872\,264.
\end{align*}
\end{theorem}

A stable Morse lower bound therefore cannot hold for all
nondegenerate Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms of closed symplectic
manifolds, even in the simply connected K\"ahler class.

\subsection*{Context and proof strategy}
The Arnold fixed-point problem asks how the critical-point constraints
of Morse theory persist for Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms
\cite{Arnold1986}. Conley and Zehnder established the torus case by
variational methods \cite{ConleyZehnder1983}, and Floer's homology
theory related periodic Hamiltonian orbits to the topology of the
ambient manifold \cite{Floer1989}. Integral refinements retain
torsion as well as rational Betti numbers. In particular, Bai and Xu
prove a lower bound using integral homology with degrees reduced
modulo twice the minimal Chern number
\cite[Theorem~A]{BaiXu2022}; see also
\cite[Corollary~1.2]{BaiXu2026}. When the minimal Chern number is
one, their expression is precisely
$\beta_{\Z}^{\mathrm{cyc}}$. Thus Theorem~\ref{thm:main}
attains this integral Floer bound.

The stable Morse number is a stronger proposed benchmark for the
Arnold problem; see \cite[Conjecture~1.2]{Golovko2020}.
Dimitroglou Rizell and Golovko prove a stable Morse lower bound for
generic Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms when both the symplectic area
class and the first Chern class vanish on $\pi_2$
\cite[Corollary~1.4]{DRG2017}. The exceptional sphere of Chern
number one in our construction excludes these hypotheses.
The classical theorem of Smale identifies $\lambda(W)$ with the
minimum number of critical points of an ordinary Morse function on a
simply connected closed manifold of sufficiently high dimension
\cite{Smale1963,Cerf1962}. The same number is a lower bound for the
geometric stable Morse number, so these two geometric minima agree
in the present setting. In contrast, a two-periodic free integral
chain complex sees the smaller count $\beta_{\Z}^{\mathrm{cyc}}$.
Our construction and its fixed-point calculation are finite-dimensional;
they do not use Floer theory.

The mixed-prime torsion and Hamiltonian involution construction of
\cite{OpenAI2026Stable} already gives a fixed-point count below the
stable Morse number. Here we change the blow-up centers to make the
count attain $\beta_{\Z}^{\mathrm{cyc}}$ exactly. We reproduce the
needed geometric arguments. A rational surface $Y$ admits a Hamiltonian
involution whose fixed set is the disjoint union of four projective
lines. For a simply connected K\"ahler manifold $X$, the product
$M=X\times Y$ therefore has an involution with four fixed
components $C=X\times\CP^1$. A small invariant Hamiltonian
perturbation replaces each component by the critical points of a
Morse function on $C$. In the dimensions used below, Smale's theorem
supplies such a function with $\lambda(C)$ critical points. The
dynamical construction therefore gives $4\lambda(C)$ nondegenerate
fixed points.

It remains to arrange
\[
 4\lambda(C)=\beta_{\Z}^{\mathrm{cyc}}(M)
 <\lambda(M).
\]
The free even homology of $\CP^1$ and $Y$ has ranks $(1,1)$ and
$(1,6,1)$, respectively. Multiplication by these spaces convolves
the torsion multiplicities of $X$ with these two sequences. We choose
$X$ so that the $3$-primary multiplicities dominate the $2$-primary
multiplicities after convolution with $(1,1)$, but not after
convolution with $(1,6,1)$. Blow-ups along seven disjoint products of
elliptic-curve quotients and projective spaces realize the required
multiplicities. This degree-sensitive choice is the mechanism that
makes the cyclic count sharp while preserving a positive degreewise
gap. It is expressed entirely in finite sequences and can be separated
from the geometric realization.

Section~\ref{sec:morse} establishes the geometric Morse comparison.
Section~\ref{sec:involution} proves the perturbation principle and
constructs $Y$. Section~\ref{sec:geometry} supplies the quotient
surfaces and the integral blow-up formula. Section~\ref{sec:construction}
chooses the centers, evaluates both counts, and proves
Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.

The extremal bodies are defined recursively. A centered nondegenerate
interval is a one-dimensional \emph{Hanner polytope}. Given Hanner
polytopes $H_1\subset\R^k$ and $H_2\subset\R^l$, their Cartesian
product and the convex hull
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 H_1\oplus_\infty H_2&=H_1\times H_2,\\
 H_1\oplus_1 H_2&=
 \conv\bigl((H_1\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times H_2)\bigr)
 \end{aligned}
\]
are Hanner polytopes in $\R^{k+l}$. These are the $\ell_\infty$ and
$\ell_1$ sums, respectively. This class contains cubes, cross-polytopes,
and mixed recursive sums. We call an invertible linear image of a
Hanner polytope a \emph{linear Hanner body}.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
For every integer $n\ge1$ and every origin-symmetric convex body
$K\subset\R^n$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:main-inequality}
 |K|\,|K^\circ|\ge\frac{4^n}{n!}.
\end{equation}
Equality holds if and only if $K$ is a linear Hanner body.
\end{theorem}

The linear equivalence in the statement respects the fixed origin
used for polarity.

\subsection{History and context}

Mahler introduced the volume-product problem in his work on convex
bodies and transference in the geometry of numbers~\cite{Mahler1939};
the planar inequality also goes back to him~\cite{MahlerPlanar1939}.
Reisner later characterized its equality cases as parallelograms,
as a consequence of his zonoid theorem~\cite[p.~340]{Reisner1986}.
Iriyeh and Shibata proved the complete three-dimensional symmetric
theorem, including equality~\cite[Theorem~1.1]{IriyehShibata}.
Fradelizi, Hubard, Meyer, Rold\'an-Pensado, and Zvavitch gave a
shorter proof based on equipartitions, together with another equality
argument and stability~\cite{FradeliziHubardMeyerRoldanZvavitch2022}.
Chen, Li, Xi, and Xu recently gave a shadow-flow proof of that theorem
in a preprint that also treats the nonsymmetric three-dimensional
problem~\cite[Theorem~7.1]{ChenLiXiXu2026}.

Hanner's recursively constructed spaces~\cite{Hanner1956} already
play a central role in the known higher-dimensional cases.
Saint-Raymond proved the sharp inequality for unconditional bodies
(those invariant under coordinate sign changes)~\cite{SaintRaymond1981};
Meyer and Reisner identified the Hanner equality cases in that
class~\cite{Meyer1986,Reisner1987}. Reisner also proved the sharp
inequality for zonoids, which are Hausdorff limits of Minkowski sums of
centered segments, and showed that equality within that class means a
parallelotope~\cite{Reisner1985,Reisner1986}; Gordon, Meyer, and
Reisner later gave a short geometric proof~\cite{GordonMeyerReisner1988}.
For local questions in Banach--Mazur distance, Nazarov, Petrov,
Ryabogin, and Zvavitch established strict local minimality, up to
linear equivalence, of the cube~\cite{NazarovPetrovRyaboginZvavitch2010}.
Kim extended this to all Hanner polytopes~\cite{Kim2014}.
Kim and Zvavitch obtained stability
in the unconditional class and the inequality in a neighborhood of
that class~\cite{KimZvavitch2015}.

A separate line of work seeks dimension-independent exponential
bounds without the sharp constant. Bourgain and Milman established
such a reverse Blaschke--Santal\'o inequality~\cite{BourgainMilman};
Kuperberg obtained an explicit stronger bound by a geometric argument
using Gauss linking integrals~\cite{Kuperberg}. Complex-analytic
approaches provide another setting for these questions. Nazarov used
H\"ormander's $\bar\partial$ theorem and Bergman kernels for the
reverse Blaschke--Santal\'o inequality~\cite{Nazarov2012}.
Berndtsson recast Kuperberg's proof using complex integrals
\cite{Berndtsson}. In a symplectic approach, Karasev proved the sharp
inequality for hyperplane sections and projections of $\ell_p$ balls

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Let $X$ be a smooth integral complex projective variety of dimension $n\ge3$,
and let $L$ be an ample line bundle. Put $V=L^n$. For a tuple
$\mathbf p=(p_1,\ldots,p_r)$ of distinct points, the ordinary multipoint
Seshadri constant is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:seshadri-definition}
 \eps(X,L;\mathbf p)
 =\inf_C\frac{L\cdot C}{\sum_{i=1}^r\mult_{p_i}C},
\end{equation}
where $C$ ranges over integral curves meeting at least one of the marked
points, and the multiplicity is zero at points outside $C$. This invariant
measures the local positivity of $L$ at the entire tuple. Its universal
upper bound is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:volume-bound}
 \eps(X,L;\mathbf p)\le (V/r)^{1/n}.
\end{equation}
Equality means that no curve imposes a stronger constraint than the volume
of $L$.

Write
\[
 U_r(X)=\{(p_1,\ldots,p_r)\in X^r:p_i\ne p_j\text{ when }i\ne j\}.
\]
A property holds at \emph{very general} tuples if the exceptional tuples
are contained in a countable union of proper Zariski-closed subsets of
$U_r(X)$.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
Let $X$ be a smooth integral complex projective variety of dimension
$n\ge3$, and let $L$ be an ample line bundle on $X$. There is an integer
$r_0=r_0(X,L)\ge1$ such that for every integer $r\ge r_0$ there is a
countable union $Z_r$ of proper Zariski-closed subsets of $U_r(X)$, with
nonempty complement, for which
\[
 \eps(X,L;\mathbf p)=\left(\frac{L^n}{r}\right)^{1/n}
 \qquad\text{for every }\mathbf p\in U_r(X)\setminus Z_r.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{samepage}
Equivalently, on the blow-up $\pi:Y\to X$ at such a tuple, with exceptional
divisors $E_1,\ldots,E_r$, the real divisor class
\[
 \pi^*L-(V/r)^{1/n}\sum_{i=1}^rE_i
\]
is nef and has top self-intersection zero. Here nefness means nonnegative
intersection with every integral curve. The threshold depends on the fixed
polarized variety, but all integers beyond it are included. In particular,
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} asserts exact equality for each such point count,
rather than convergence of a normalized constant as $r$ increases.
\end{samepage}

\subsection{Background and relation to earlier work}

The plane problem originates in Nagata's work on Hilbert's fourteenth
problem. He conjectured a lower bound on the degree of a plane curve in
terms of its multiplicities at very general points, and proved the strict
inequality when the number of points is a square at least $16$
\cite{Nagata1959}. Multipoint Seshadri constants express the corresponding
positivity question on an arbitrary polarized variety. The qualitative
Nagata--Biran--Szemberg formulation asks for maximality at every sufficiently
large point count. Ro\'e and Ross state this formulation in arbitrary
dimension and distinguish the ordinary curve-defined constant from its
higher-cycle analogues \cite[Conjecture~1.3 and Remark~1.4]{RoeRoss2009}.
We use the ordinary constant throughout, even when $\dim X>2$.

Biran's packing stability theorem supplies an important symplectic
precedent: sufficiently many equal balls can fill a closed symplectic
four-manifold with rational symplectic class with arbitrarily small volume
deficit \cite{Biran1999}; see also \cite[Theorem~6.3]{Biran2001}. The algebraic
question fixes the complex variety and asks for a nef class on its point
blow-ups, so symplectic packing stability is not by itself the required
algebraic statement. In arbitrary dimension, K\"uchle obtained lower bounds
for multipoint Seshadri constants that are asymptotically optimal as the
number of points tends to infinity \cite[Theorem~1.1]{Kuechle1996}.
Biran's product inequality, extended to higher-cycle constants by
Ro\'e--Ross, relates point counts on a variety to point counts on projective
space \cite[Theorem~1.1 and Remark~1.2]{RoeRoss2009}.
These results illuminate the volume scale in \eqref{eq:volume-bound}; an
asymptotically optimal estimate alone does not imply eventual equality.

The companion paper \cite{OpenAI2026Surfaces} establishes the qualitative
surface statement by a nodal exponent bound, diagonal slice compression,
and a primitive lattice direction tuned to the number of points. Its final
tests are \emph{injective} jet evaluations on finite torus subgroups.
We adapt the planar geometric mechanism to polynomial spaces in two
variables and use \emph{surjective} full-dimensional jet evaluations instead.
All arguments required for this adaptation are proved here; the surface
maximality theorem is not an input.

The interpretation of positivity through asymptotic jet generation is
classical; see Demailly \cite[Section~6]{Demailly1992}.
Our use of initial monomials belongs to the valuation approach to linear
series initiated by Okounkov \cite{Okounkov1996} and developed by Lazarsfeld--Musta\c{t}\u{a}
\cite{LazarsfeldMustata2009} and Kaveh--Khovanskii
\cite{KavehKhovanskii2012}. More directly, Ito compares multipoint jet
separation with initial monomial spaces by separate finite-degree
degenerations, without a finite-generation hypothesis
\cite[Proposition~5.7 and Theorem~5.8]{Ito2013}.
Monomial diagrams and interpolation minors also underlie Dumnicki's
diagram-cutting method \cite[Proposition~13 and Theorem~14]{Dumnicki2007}.
We retain elementary proofs of the specific transfer and counting statements
used below.

\subsection{Proof strategy and the two-coordinate construction}

Separating jets through degree $m$ at a tuple means prescribing,
independently at each point, all Taylor coefficients of total degree at
most $m$, in local coordinates and line-bundle frames. If $H^0(X,kL)$
separates these jets, then
\[
 \eps(X,L;\mathbf p)\ge \frac{m}{k};
\]
the curve-intersection argument is given in Lemma~\ref{lem:jets-curves}.
Thus, for $w=(V/r)^{1/n}$, our interpolation target is jet separation
through degree $\lfloor k\theta\rfloor$ for every fixed $0<\theta<w$
and all sufficiently large $k$. We first construct a tuple for each such
test and later obtain simultaneous tests at very general tuples.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Arnold's fixed-point conjecture compares Hamiltonian dynamics with the
critical-point theory of smooth functions. For a sufficiently short
autonomous Hamiltonian flow on a closed symplectic manifold, its fixed points are
exactly the critical points of its Hamiltonian. The conjecture asks
whether an arbitrary Hamiltonian diffeomorphism must retain the minimum
number of critical points forced by the topology of the manifold.
Arnold's formulation explicitly includes the count of geometrically
distinct points~\cite[Section~2]{Arnold1986}. We construct a smooth
counterexample on the complex quadric threefold, which also violates the
weaker rational cup-length bound.

\paragraph{The two degenerate bounds.}
For a closed smooth manifold $M$, write
\[
 \CritSet(h)=\{q\in M:dh_q=0\},\qquad
 \Crit(M)=\min_{h\in C^\infty(M,\R)}\#\CritSet(h).
\]
The minimum here permits degenerate critical points, whereas the
\emph{Morse number} minimizes only over Morse functions. Let
$\operatorname{cuplength}(M;\mathbb Q)$ be one plus the maximum number
of positive-degree rational cohomology classes with nonzero cup product.
Thus our cup-length convention includes the unit. The
Lusternik--Schnirelmann inequality gives
\[
 \operatorname{cuplength}(M;\mathbb Q)\le\Crit(M);
\]
Section~\ref{sec:critical-bound} recalls the cup-product argument in a
form that applies to arbitrary smooth functions.

A Hamiltonian diffeomorphism of a symplectic manifold $(M,\omega)$ is
the time-one map of a smooth time-dependent Hamiltonian flow. We write
$\Ham(M,\omega)$ for these maps, use the convention
$\iota_{X_{H_t}}\omega=dH_t$, and set
$\Fix(\phi)=\{q\in M:\phi(q)=q\}$.
The \emph{critical-number Arnold bound} asserts that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:arnold-bound}
 \#\Fix(\phi)\ge\Crit(M)
\end{equation}
for every $\phi\in\Ham(M,\omega)$ on every closed connected symplectic
manifold. Its weaker \emph{rational cup-length} form replaces $\Crit(M)$
by $\operatorname{cuplength}(M;\mathbb Q)$. Neither formulation assumes
nondegeneracy; see Golovko~\cite[Conjectures~1.4 and~1.6]{Golovko2020}.
A fixed point $q$ is nondegenerate when $1$ is not an eigenvalue of
$d\phi_q$.

Let
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quadric}
 Q^3=\bigl\{[z_0:z_1:z_2:z_3:z_4]\in\CP^4:
                 z_0^2+z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2+z_4^2=0\bigr\},
\end{equation}
with the restricted Fubini--Study symplectic form, normalized in
Section~\ref{sec:quadric}.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:counterexample}
There is a smooth Hamiltonian diffeomorphism $\phi$ of the closed connected
symplectic six-manifold $Q^3$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:counterexample}
 \#\Fix(\phi)=3<4=\Crit(Q^3)
                  =\operatorname{cuplength}(Q^3;\mathbb Q).
\end{equation}
At least one fixed point of $\phi$ is degenerate.
\end{theorem}

This disproves both unrestricted smooth bounds. The count includes all
fixed points, so imposing a contractibility condition on their
Hamiltonian trajectories cannot restore either inequality. The
nondegenerate homological Arnold inequalities concern a different
hypothesis and remain compatible with this example.

The count of three is sharp. Gong~\cite[Section~1.1.1]{Gong2025}
obtains at least $n$ fixed points for every Hamiltonian diffeomorphism
of the standard complex quadric of complex dimension $n\ge2$.
His normalization of the Fubini--Study form differs from ours by a
positive scalar, which does not change the Hamiltonian group: rescaling
the form and a generating Hamiltonian by the same scalar preserves its
vector field. Thus our example attains his bound for $n=3$.

\paragraph{Historical context and related work.}
The positive cases explain why the unrestricted comparison is natural.
Conley and Zehnder proved that every Hamiltonian diffeomorphism of the
standard symplectic torus $T^{2n}$ has at least $2n+1$ fixed
points~\cite{ConleyZehnder1983}, and Fortune obtained the bound $n+1$
on standard $\CP^n$~\cite{Fortune1985}. Hofer obtained cup-length bounds without
nondegeneracy when $\pi_2(M)=0$~\cite[Theorem~4]{Hofer1988}.
Rudyak and Oprea proved the full critical-number bound when both the
symplectic class and the first Chern class vanish on $\pi_2(M)$
\cite[Corollary~4.3]{RudyakOprea1999}. The quadric has spheres of
positive symplectic area and lies outside these latter hypotheses.

Floer's pseudoholomorphic-curve methods established homological Morse
inequalities for nondegenerate Hamiltonian fixed points, including the
monotone setting~\cite{Floer1989}. The lower bound by the sum of rational
Betti numbers was subsequently established for nondegenerate Hamiltonian
diffeomorphisms on every closed symplectic manifold by Fukaya and Ono,
Liu and Tian, and Ruan~\cite{FukayaOno1999,LiuTian1998,Ruan1999}.
The distinction between these bounds
and the degenerate formulations above is essential; see
\cite[Theorem~1.3 and Conjectures~1.4 and~1.6]{Golovko2020}.
Ma~\cite[Theorem~1.5]{Ma2013} asserted that the minimum number of fixed
points over all Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms always equals $\Crit(M)$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:counterexample} contradicts that assertion.

Regularity also matters. Buhovsky, Humili\`ere, and Seyfaddini constructed
Hamiltonian \emph{homeomorphisms} with a single fixed point on every closed
connected symplectic manifold of real dimension at least four
\cite{BHS2018}. Our construction stays in the smooth Hamiltonian group.
In a preprint posted September 27, 2026, Jiao~\cite[Theorem~1.1]{Jiao2026}
reports a smooth Hamiltonian diffeomorphism of the equal-area product
$S^2\times S^2$ with two fixed points, using local saddle merging and
mixed generating functions. The construction here instead uses a
finite-order map on a six-dimensional quadric. None of these
fixed-point results is an input to our construction.

\paragraph{Proof mechanism.}
The key is to transfer a critical-point count from a fixed submanifold
to the fixed-point count of a nearby Hamiltonian map. Let $A$ be a
finite-order Hamiltonian map with fixed submanifold $F$, whose fixed
tangent vectors are exactly those tangent to $F$. Extend a function
$f$ on $F$ to an $A$-invariant function $K$ on the ambient manifold,
and let $B_s$ be its Hamiltonian flow. If $A^m=\id$, invariance gives
\[
 (A\circ B_\varepsilon)^m=B_{m\varepsilon}.
\]
For sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, the right side has only
stationary fixed points. Any fixed point of $A\circ B_\varepsilon$
is therefore a critical point of $K$ fixed by $A$. Finite-group
averaging makes ambient criticality on $F$ equivalent to criticality
of $f$, giving
\[
 \Fix(A\circ B_\varepsilon)=\CritSet(f).
\]
This criticality step is the finite-group case of Palais's principle
of symmetric criticality~\cite[Section~5]{Palais1979}; the power identity
excludes additional fixed points away from $F$.

For the quadric, take the Hamiltonian involution
\[
 A[z_0:z_1:z_2:z_3:z_4]=[z_0:-z_1:-z_2:-z_3:-z_4].
\]
Its fixed locus is the quadric surface $Q^2\cong S^2\times S^2$.
This product admits functions with only three critical points, as
recorded by Mare~\cite[Proposition~3.2.5]{Mare1997} through an extension
of Takens's sphere-product construction~\cite{Takens1968}. We give an
explicit formula and compute its entire critical set. The isolated
degenerate critical point becomes a degenerate Hamiltonian fixed point.
In contrast, symplectic volume forces every smooth function on the
ambient $Q^3$ to have at least four critical points, and a Hamiltonian
rotation realizes that minimum.

Section~\ref{sec:reduction} proves the finite-order transfer, including
the short-period estimate and invariant extension.
Section~\ref{sec:quadric} constructs the Hamiltonian involution and
its tangent splitting. Section~\ref{sec:three-points} gives the
three-critical-point function. Section~\ref{sec:critical-bound}
proves the critical-number and rational cup-length equalities on $Q^3$,
and Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} assembles the construction and
verifies degeneracy.

\section{Perturbing a finite-order Hamiltonian map}
\label{sec:reduction}

A short Hamiltonian perturbation of a finite-order map can replace its
fixed submanifold by the critical set of a function on that submanifold.
The tangent-space hypothesis below is the usual \emph{clean fixed-set}
condition; we state it explicitly to identify the geometric input.

\begin{proposition}
\label{prop:reduction}
Let \((M,\omega)\) be a closed symplectic manifold, and let
\(A\in\Ham(M,\omega)\) satisfy \(A^m=\id\) for some positive integer
\(m\). Suppose that \(F=\Fix(A)\) is a closed embedded submanifold and
that
\[
  T_qF=\ker(dA_q-\id)
  \qquad\text{for every }q\in F.
\]
For every smooth function \(f:F\to\R\), there is a smooth
\(A\)-invariant extension \(K:M\to\R\) such that, if \(B_s\) is its
Hamiltonian flow, then for every sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\)
the map
\[
  \phi_\varepsilon=A\circ B_\varepsilon
\]
is Hamiltonian and satisfies
\[
  \Fix(\phi_\varepsilon)=\CritSet(f),
\]
where the critical set on the right is viewed as a subset of \(M\).
\end{proposition}

The proof combines finite-group averaging with the exclusion of short
nonconstant periodic trajectories. We establish the latter fact first.
Lipschitz control of a vector field gives a lower bound for its
nonconstant periods, a classical principle for which Yorke proved the
sharp Euclidean estimate~\cite{Yorke1969}. The following elementary
local argument suffices here.

\begin{lemma}
\label{lem:short-periods}
Let \(X\) be a smooth vector field on a closed manifold \(M\), and let
\(\Psi_t\) be its flow. There is a number \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
  \Fix(\Psi_t)=\{q\in M:X(q)=0\}
  \qquad\text{for every }0<t<\delta.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The flow is defined for all time because \(M\) is compact. Suppose that
there were points \(q_j\) and times \(t_j>0\) with
\[
  t_j\longrightarrow0,\qquad
  \Psi_{t_j}(q_j)=q_j,\qquad X(q_j)\ne0.
\]
After passing to a subsequence, assume that \(q_j\to q\). Choose
coordinates near \(q\), and a Euclidean ball about its coordinate image
whose closure lies inside the coordinate domain. By continuity of the
flow, all sufficiently late trajectory segments
\(\{\Psi_s(q_j):0\le s\le t_j\}\) lie in this ball. The coordinate vector
field \(V\) is Lipschitz there with a constant \(L\ge0\), since its
derivative is bounded on the closed ball.

Write \(u_j(s)\) for the coordinate trajectory and set
\[
  C_j=\max_{0\le s\le t_j}|\dot u_j(s)|>0.
\]
For any \(s,r\in[0,t_j]\), convexity of the ball and the Lipschitz
estimate give
\[
 \begin{split}
  |\dot u_j(s)-\dot u_j(r)|
   &=|V(u_j(s))-V(u_j(r))|\\
   &\le L|u_j(s)-u_j(r)|
    \le LC_j|s-r|
    \le LC_jt_j.
 \end{split}
\]
The closed trajectory has zero mean coordinate velocity:
\(\int_0^{t_j}\dot u_j(r)\,dr=0\). At a time \(s_j\) of maximum speed,
it follows that
\[
  C_j
  =\left|
     \frac1{t_j}\int_0^{t_j}
        \bigl(\dot u_j(s_j)-\dot u_j(r)\bigr)\,dr
    \right|
  \le LC_jt_j.
\]
Dividing by \(C_j\) contradicts \(t_j\to0\). Thus all fixed points of a
sufficiently short positive-time map are zeros of \(X\). Conversely,
every zero of \(X\) is stationary and hence fixed by every \(\Psi_t\).
\end{proof}

\section{The Morse-number question}\label{sec:introduction}
Arnold's fixed-point conjectures compare Hamiltonian fixed points with
critical points of functions on the underlying symplectic manifold
\cite[Section~2]{Arnold1986}. For a sufficiently $C^2$-small autonomous Hamiltonian,
the fixed points of its time-one map are precisely its critical points.
The question is how much of this finite-dimensional lower bound survives
for an arbitrary Hamiltonian path. We address the formulation using the
ordinary Morse number.

Let $(M,\omega)$ be a closed connected symplectic manifold and let
$H\in C^\infty((\R/\Z)\times M,\R)$. We use the convention
\[
 \omega(X_H(t,\cdot),\cdot)=dH_t,
 \qquad \phi_H^0=\mathrm{id}_M
\]
for the Hamiltonian vector field and its flow. A fixed point $x$ of
$\phi_H^1$ is \emph{nondegenerate} if
$1\notin\Spec(d_x\phi_H^1)$. Write $\Fix_0(\phi_H^1;H)$ for the fixed
points whose loops $t\mapsto\phi_H^t(x)$ are contractible in $M$.
Contractibility here refers to this Hamiltonian path.

The \emph{ordinary Morse number} is
\[
 \Morse(M)=\min\{\#\Crit(f):f\in C^\infty(M,\R)\text{ is Morse}\}.
\]
The Morse-number form of the Arnold conjecture asks whether
$\#\Fix_0(\phi_H^1;H)\ge\Morse(M)$ whenever the time-one map is
nondegenerate \cite[Conjecture~1.1]{Golovko2020}.
We construct examples in which even the total number of fixed points is
smaller than $\Morse(M)$, and every fixed-point trajectory is contractible.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
There exist a closed connected symplectic manifold $(M,\omega)$ of real
dimension twelve and a smooth one-periodic Hamiltonian $H$ such that every
fixed point of $\phi_H^1$ is nondegenerate and
\[
\#\Fix_0(\phi_H^1;H)=\#\Fix(\phi_H^1)
                   =\chi(M)+128<\Morse(M).
\]
\end{theorem}

The same construction gives a quantitative separation in fixed dimension.
\begin{corollary}\label{cor:deficit}
For every real number $D>0$, there is an example as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} satisfying
\[
 \Morse(M)-\#\Fix(\phi_H^1)>D.
\]
The manifold is allowed to depend on $D$.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{From homological bounds to ordinary Morse theory}
Conley and Zehnder proved the nondegenerate bound on the standard
symplectic torus, where the ordinary Morse number equals the total Betti
number~\cite{ConleyZehnder1983}.
Floer's pseudoholomorphic-curve approach established homological Morse
inequalities for Hamiltonian fixed points, including the monotone
setting~\cite{Floer1989}. Virtual-moduli constructions of Fukaya--Ono,
Liu--Tian and Ruan extended the rational Betti-number bound to general
closed symplectic manifolds
\cite{FukayaOno1999,LiuTian1998,Ruan1999}.
The integral bounds of Bai--Xu retain torsion information as well
\cite[Theorem~A]{BaiXu2022}, \cite[Corollary~1.2]{BaiXu2026}.
These homological bounds do not identify the number of generators of a
Floer complex with the minimum number of critical points of an ordinary
Morse function.

Stabilization explains one source of this distinction. The
\emph{stable Morse number} minimizes the number of critical points of
Morse functions $F:M\times\R^r\to\R$ that are almost quadratic at
infinity, allowing the integer $r\geq0$ to vary. Here this means that $\|dF-dQ\|$ is
uniformly bounded in a product metric for some nondegenerate quadratic
form $Q$ on $\R^r$~\cite[Section~2.1]{DRG2017}.
Arnold already considered a related stable critical-point minimum and
asked whether it equals the minimum on the original manifold
\cite[Section~5]{Arnold1986}.
Eliashberg and Gromov developed the relationship with simple chain
homotopy over the fundamental-group ring and augmentation-ideal
generation~\cite[Sections~0.2.2 and~0.2.5]{EliashbergGromov1998}.
Damian proved that ordinary and stable Morse numbers of closed manifolds
can differ~\cite{Damian2002}. A relative realization theorem after
sufficiently large stabilization is given in
\cite[Proposition~2.9]{DRG2018}.

The algebraic distinction used here is classical and particularly sharp
for direct powers of nontrivial perfect finite groups. Cossey, Gruenberg and
Kov\'acs proved that the augmentation-ideal generator number remains
constant under these direct powers, while the group generator number
is unbounded~\cite[Theorems~1--2]{CGK1974}; see also
\cite[Sections~1--2]{GruenbergLinnell}.
Fundamental-group refinements of Floer theory reflect this distinction:
Ono--Pajitnov obtain augmentation-ideal bounds under weak monotonicity
\cite[Theorem~5.7]{OnoPajitnov2016}, whereas, in the symplectically
aspherical or monotone setting, Barraud's reconstruction of group
generators counts Floer trajectories with multiplicities
\cite[Theorem~1.3 and Remark~3]{Barraud2018}.
The trajectory multiplicities are part of the bound; these results do
not yield the unrestricted ordinary Morse-number inequality.

For closed symplectic manifolds on which both $[\omega]$ and $c_1(TM)$
vanish on $\pi_2(M)$, Dimitroglou Rizell and Golovko prove the stable
Morse number as a lower bound for nondegenerate Hamiltonian fixed
points~\cite[Corollary~1.3]{DRG2017}.
The sphere factors in our examples have positive symplectic area, so
this hypothesis does not hold. The construction below instead realizes
a short relative Morse complex in exactly eight additional variables,
with the function equal to a prescribed quadratic form outside a compact
set. Its small-time return map is then inserted into a closed product
of spheres. The relative handle realization and the exclusion of all
additional fixed points are the two geometric steps needed to turn the
ordinary/stable distinction into the stated closed Hamiltonian example.

The integral homology of our examples is torsion-free and concentrated
in even degrees, with total rank $\chi(M)$, as verified in
Section~\ref{sec:counting}. Their fixed-point count therefore exceeds
the homological quantities above.

Ma's preprint asserts that the minimum number of fixed points of a
nondegenerate Hamiltonian diffeomorphism always equals the ordinary
Morse number~\cite[Theorem~1.5]{Ma2013}. Theorem~\ref{thm:main}
contradicts that unrestricted assertion.

\subsection{The construction and its two counts}
For a finitely generated group $G$, let $d(G)$ be the least number of group
generators. Set $b=2$ and consider the finite groups $G=A_5^k$, where
$A_5$ has order $60$. Two elementary algebraic facts will drive the proof:
$d(A_5^k)$ is unbounded as $k$ increases, whereas the right augmentation
ideal
\[
 I_G=\ker(\aug:\Z[G]\longrightarrow\Z)
\]
has a generating list of length $b$, independent of $k$.
The distinction is between generation of a group and generation of a
module over its group ring.

Gompf's existence theorem supplies a closed connected symplectic
four-manifold $X$ with $\pi_1(X)=G$~\cite[Theorem~3.1]{Gompf1992};
see also \cite{Gompf1995}.
We construct a Morse function on $X\times\R^8$ with precisely
$\chi(X)+4b$ critical points, equal outside a compact set to the quadratic
form of index four
\[
 Q(u,v)=\frac{|v|^2-|u|^2}{2},\qquad u,v\in\R^4.
\]
The eight variables are fixed throughout: the proof performs handle moves
on one twelve-dimensional cobordism, rather than appealing to a
stabilization of unspecified dimension.

The closed symplectic manifold is
$M=X\times(S^2)^4$. Sixteen disjoint product-cap neighborhoods correspond
to the north/south choices on the four sphere factors. We place the same
small-time return map of the constructed Morse function in each cap.
The main gluing issue is to match the local \emph{endpoint} with product
rotations at both poles while excluding fixed points outside the caps.
The resulting smooth one-periodic Hamiltonian satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:overview-fixed-count}
 \#\Fix(\phi_H^1)=16\bigl(\chi(X)+4b\bigr)
                   =\chi(M)+128.
\end{equation}

On the other hand, the fundamental group forces every Morse function on
$M$ to have at least $d(G)$ critical points in each of indices one and
eleven. Euler's identity gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:overview-morse-bound}
 \Morse(M)\ge\chi(M)+4d(G).
\end{equation}
Since $d(A_5^k)$ is unbounded while $b$ is fixed, these two estimates
give the strict inequality and the arbitrary deficits. Figure~\ref{fig:construction}
separates the two roles of the fundamental group.

\begin{figure}[ht]
\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[
 every node/.style={align=center,font=\small},
 box/.style={draw,inner sep=6pt,text width=58mm},
 >={Stealth}]
\node[box,text width=90mm] (group) at (0,0)
{$G=A_5^k$\\$I_G$ has two generators; $d(G)$ is unbounded};
\node[box] (morse) at (-3.4,-1.8)

\node[box] (bound) at (3.4,-1.8)

\node[box] (closed) at (-3.4,-3.6)

\label{fig:construction}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Proof organization}
Section~\ref{sec:algebra} proves the two group-ring facts and the exact
row operation needed for geometric cancellation.
Section~\ref{sec:relative-model} constructs the relative Morse model and
its handle complex. Section~\ref{sec:cancellation} reduces the handle
counts while preserving the quadratic collars.
Section~\ref{sec:hamiltonian} realizes the local map on the closed product.
Section~\ref{sec:counting} compares the two counts and proves the theorem
and its deficit corollary.

\section{Closing the Hamiltonian model}
\label{sec:hamiltonian}

We now turn a Morse function with eight quadratic variables into a
Hamiltonian map on a closed manifold.  Each of the sixteen products of
north and south sphere caps will contain one copy of its critical set.
The rotations outside the caps must be chosen with care: their endpoint
maps agree with the quadratic model at both poles, although their paths
can differ by full turns. We track this difference to identify the
homotopy classes of the resulting fixed-point loops as well.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:cap-transfer}
Let $(X,\omega_X)$ be a closed connected symplectic four-manifold. Write
$(u,v)\in\R^4\times\R^4$ and set
\[
 Q(u,v)=\frac{|v|^2-|u|^2}{2},
 \qquad r^2=|u|^2+|v|^2.
\]
Suppose that $F\colon X\times\R^8\to\R$ is a smooth Morse function
such that $F=Q$ whenever $r\ge3$, and let $N=\#\Crit(F)$.
Let $\sigma$ be the standard area form of total area $4\pi$ on the unit
sphere. For every $\lambda>25/2$, the closed symplectic manifold
\[
 (M,\omega_M)=
 \left(X\times(S^2)^4,
 \omega_X+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^4\sigma_j\right)
\]
admits a Hamiltonian $H\in C^\infty((\R/\mathbb Z)\times M,\R)$ such
that every fixed point of $\phi_H^1$ is nondegenerate, every loop
$t\mapsto\phi_H^t(p)$ based at a fixed point $p$ is contractible in
$M$, and
\[
 \#\Fix_0(\phi_H^1;H)=\#\Fix(\phi_H^1)=16N.
\]
Here $\sigma_j$ denotes the pullback of $\sigma$ from the $j$th sphere,
and Hamiltonian vector fields satisfy $\omega_M(X_H,\cdot)=dH$.
\end{proposition}

We first record the local short-period estimate used below. Yorke proved
the sharp lower bound $2\pi/L$ for a nonconstant periodic solution of a
Euclidean vector field with Lipschitz constant $L$~\cite{Yorke1969}.
The weaker coordinate estimate here suffices on a compact invariant set.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:short-period}
Let $V$ be a smooth vector field on a smooth manifold, with flow
$\Phi^t$, and let $K$ be a compact set on which this flow is defined
for all times and which it preserves. There is a number $\tau_0>0$
such that, for $p\in K$ and $0<\tau<\tau_0$,
\[
 \Phi^\tau(p)=p\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad V(p)=0.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose finitely many charts with image the Euclidean ball of radius
$3$, whose inverse images of the unit ball cover $K$. Let $C\ge1$
bound both the coordinate vector fields and their first derivatives
on the closed balls of radius $2$, and put $\tau_0=1/(2C)$.
If $0<\tau<\tau_0$, a trajectory
$t\mapsto\Phi^{\tau t}(p)$, $0\le t\le1$, with $p\in K$ stays
in the radius-$2$ ball of a chart whose unit ball contains $p$:
a first exit would require coordinate displacement greater than $1$,
whereas the speed bound gives displacement at most $\tau C<1/2$.
If the trajectory is a loop, write $w$ for its coordinate expression
and $\widehat V$ for the coordinate vector field. Then
\[
 \dot w(t)=\tau\widehat V(w(t)),\qquad
 \int_0^1\widehat V(w(t))\,dt=0.
\]
Set $S=\max_t|\widehat V(w(t))|$. Since
$|w(t)-w(a)|\le\tau S$ for $a,t\in[0,1]$, subtracting the zero
average and using the Lipschitz bound on this convex ball gives
\[
 |\widehat V(w(t))|
 \le\int_0^1|\widehat V(w(t))-\widehat V(w(a))|\,da
 \le C\tau S.
\]
Thus $S=0$, so the loop is constant and $V(p)=0$. The converse follows
from uniqueness of solutions. No homotopy assumption on the loop is used.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:cap-transfer}]
\emph{The local flows.}
Identify $\R^8$ with $\C^4$ by writing
\[
 u=(x_1,y_1,x_2,y_2),\qquad
 v=(x_3,y_3,x_4,y_4),\qquad z_j=x_j+iy_j,
\]
and equip $X\times\C^4$ with
$\Omega=\omega_X+\sum_jdx_j\wedge dy_j$.

1. Introduction
1.1. Ball packing stability
Consider a connected symplectic manifold (M2​n,ω)(M^{2n},\omega) of finite volume, which may be open or have boundary. For k≥1k\geq 1, the kk-th ball packing number of MM, denoted by pk​(M)p_{k}(M), quantifies how much of the volume of MM can be covered by kk disjoint, symplectically embedded balls of equal size. More precisely, the numbers pk​(M)p_{k}(M) are defined by
pk​(M)≔supak⋅vol⁡(B⁡(a))vol⁡(M)∈[0,1],p_{k}(M)\coloneqq\sup_{a}\frac{k\cdot\operatorname{vol}(B(a))}{\operatorname{vol}(M)}\in[0,1],
where the supremum is taken over all a>0a>0 such that the disjoint union of kk copies of the closed 2​n2n-dimensional ball B​(a)=B2​n​(a)B(a)=B^{2n}(a) of symplectic width aa admits a symplectic embedding into the interior of MM. The ball packing numbers serve as a fundamental quantitative measure of symplectic rigidity. Since Gromov’s seminal work [Gro85], which revealed the first non-trivial obstructions to symplectic embeddings, these invariants have attracted considerable attention. We refer to [Sch, Hut11b, CHLS07] for surveys.
In [MP94, Remark 1.5.G], McDuff and Polterovich observed that limk→∞pk​(M)=1\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}p_{k}(M)=1 for every symplectic manifold of finite volume. This implies that symplectic ball packings become asymptotically flexible as the number of balls increases. In [Bir97, Bir99], Biran proved a much stronger and deeper flexibility result for closed, connected symplectic 44-manifolds (M4,ω)(M^{4},\omega) which are rational, meaning that the symplectic form ω\omega represents a rational cohomology class [ω]∈H2​(M,ℚ)[\omega]\in H^{2}(M;\mathbb{Q}). He showed that there exists a finite threshold k0k_{0}, depending on MM, such that pk​(M)=1p_{k}(M)=1 for all k≥k0k\geq k_{0}. This phenomenon is referred to as symplectic ball packing stability.
A natural problem is to determine which connected symplectic manifolds of finite volume, beyond closed, rational symplectic 44-manifolds, exhibit packing stability. This question is explicitly raised in the survey article [CHLS07, §3.2, Problem 4] by Cieliebak, Latschev, Hofer, and Schlenk, as well as in [Sch, Conjecture 13.2] by Schlenk. Several results have been established in this direction. It was proved by Buse and Hind [BH11, BH13] that packing stability holds for closed, rational symplectic manifolds of arbitrary dimension. In dimension four, Buse, Hind, and Opshtein [BHO16] eliminated the rationality assumption, showing that packing stability holds for all closed, connected symplectic 44-manifolds. In higher dimensions, however, the general case remains open. Moreover, packing stability has been verified for certain open manifolds with highly symmetric boundary, including balls and ellipsoids [BH13], 44-dimensional polydisks and pseudoballs [BHO16], and 44-dimensional rational convex toric domains [CHMP25].
In contrast to the positive results described above, Cristofaro-Gardiner and Hind [CHa] recently identified the first examples of open symplectic manifolds of finite volume for which packing stability fails. They constructed open domains U⊂ℝ4U\subset\mathbb{R}^{4}, diffeomorphic to the open 44-ball, such that pk​(U)<1p_{k}(U)<1 for all k≥1k\geq 1. The failure of packing stability in these examples is connected to the domains’ “wild” boundary behaviour; see Subsection 1.3 below for further discussion. This leaves a significant gap between these counterexamples and the known cases of packing stability, i.e. closed manifolds and special toric domains. It is an intriguing problem to more precisely identify and understand the transition between packing stability and its failure.
An important question is whether packing stability holds for compact symplectic manifolds with smooth boundary; see [CHa, Question 7.1]. The known cases involving toric boundary provide limited insight into what one might expect in the general setting. For example, the symplectic 44-ball B4​(1)B^{4}(1) is symplectomorphic to the complement of a line in ℂ​P2\mathbb{C}P^{2}, equipped with a suitably scaled Fubini–Study symplectic form. More generally, any 44-dimensional convex toric domain can be approximated by toric domains which are symplectomorphic to the complements of nodal divisors in closed symplectic 44-manifolds; see [Cri19]. In other words, the known instances of packing stability in the presence of boundary essentially reduce to the case of nodal divisor complements and thus do not substantially extend beyond the closed case. In particular, no examples are known of packing stability for symplectic manifolds whose boundary carries a characteristic foliation with chaotic behaviour. In fact, general symplectic embedding results for manifolds with dynamically rich boundaries are rare; see [Edt24] for an exception.
A major motivation for studying ball packings in symplectic manifolds with general smooth boundary arises from a close connection to the asymptotic behaviour of certain sequences of symplectic spectral invariants; see Subsection 1.4 below. These invariants encode important dynamical information, making manifolds with boundary—where the dynamics occurs—central to our investigation. Our first main result establishes that packing stability holds for all compact, connected symplectic 44-manifolds with smooth boundary.
Theorem A (Ball packing stability).
Let (M4,ω)(M^{4},\omega) be a compact, connected symplectic 44-manifold, possibly with smooth boundary. Then symplectic ball packing stability holds for MM. This means that there exists a positive integer k0k_{0} such that pk​(M)=1p_{k}(M)=1 for all k≥k0k\geq k_{0}.
We note that in Theorem A we only assume that the boundary is smooth and in particular do not impose any contact type assumptions.
1.2. Ellipsoid embedding stability
Recall that the symplectic ellipsoid E⁡(a1,…,an)E(a_{1},\dots,a_{n}) with widths ai>0a_{i}>0 is defined by
E⁡(a1,…,an)≔{z∈ℂn|∑jπ​|zj|2aj≤1},E(a_{1},\dots,a_{n})\coloneqq\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}^{n}\kern 5.0pt\Big|\kern 5.0pt\sum_{j}\frac{\pi|z_{j}|^{2}}{a_{j}}\leq 1\right\},
where ℝ2​n≅ℂn\mathbb{R}^{2n}\cong\mathbb{C}^{n} is equipped with the standard symplectic form ω0=∑id​xi∧d​yi\omega_{0}=\sum_{i}dx_{i}\wedge dy_{i}. Let (M2​n,ω)(M^{2n},\omega) be a connected symplectic manifold of finite volume. For every real number a≥1a\geq 1, the ellipsoid embedding number paE​(M)p_{a}^{E}(M) quantifies how much of the volume of MM can be filled by a single symplectic ellipsoid obtained from E⁡(1,…,1,a)E(1,\dots,1,a) by scaling. It is defined by
paE​(M)≔supλvol⁡(E⁡(λ,…,λ,λ​a))vol⁡(M)∈[0,1],p_{a}^{E}(M)\coloneqq\sup_{\lambda}\frac{\operatorname{vol}(E(\lambda,\dots,\lambda,\lambda a))}{\operatorname{vol}(M)}\in[0,1],
where the supremum is taken over all positive numbers λ>0\lambda>0 such that the ellipsoid E⁡(λ,…,λ,λ​a)E(\lambda,\dots,\lambda,\lambda a) admits a symplectic embedding into the interior of MM; see [Sch05b, §1.3.2]. Since the ellipsoid E⁡(a,…,a)E(a,\dots,a) is simply the ball B⁡(a)B(a), we have p1E​(M)=p1​(M)p_{1}^{E}(M)=p_{1}(M). It is well known that, for every positive integer k≥1k\geq 1, the ellipsoid E⁡(1,…,1,k)E(1,\dots,1,k) can be fully packed by kk balls of equal size. This implies that pkE​(M)≤pk​(M)p_{k}^{E}(M)\leq p_{k}(M) for all k≥1k\geq 1.
Schlenk proved in [Sch05b, §1.3.2, Theorem 3] that, for every connected symplectic manifold MM of finite volume, we have lima→∞paE​(M)=1\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty}p_{a}^{E}(M)=1. In other words, symplectic embeddings of ellipsoids into MM become asymptotically flexible as the ellipsoids become increasingly skinny. We say that ellipsoid embedding stability holds for MM if there exists a finite threshold a0a_{0} such that paE​(M)=1p_{a}^{E}(M)=1 for all a≥a0a\geq a_{0}.
Since ball packing stability holds for every ellipsoid, the condition paE​(M)=1p_{a}^{E}(M)=1 for even a single value of aa implies ball packing stability. In particular, ellipsoid embedding stability implies ball packing stability. Moreover, it was shown in [BH13, Theorem 1.1] that ellipsoid embedding stability holds for every ellipsoid, so knowing that paE​(M)=1p_{a}^{E}(M)=1 for one value of aa also implies ellipsoid embedding stability.
It follows from [Bir01] and [Ops13]—see also [BH13, Theorem 1.3]—that every closed, connected, rational symplectic manifold MM can be fully filled by one single ellipsoid; that is paE​(M)=1p_{a}^{E}(M)=1 for some a≥1a\geq 1. This means that ellipsoid embedding stability holds for such manifolds. While ball packing stability is known to hold for all closed symplectic 44-manifolds [BHO16], the corresponding statement for ellipsoid embedding stability is open; see [BHO16, Conjecture 1] and [Sch, Conjecture 13.8].
We prove that our ball packing stability result (Theorem A) can, in fact, be strengthened to ellipsoid embedding stability. Although this result is new even in the closed case, the primary case of interest concerns compact symplectic manifolds whose boundary exhibits rich dynamical behaviour.
Theorem B (Ellipsoid embedding stability).
Let (M4,ω)(M^{4},\omega) be a compact, connected symplectic 44-manifold, possibly with smooth boundary. Then symplectic ellipsoid embedding stability holds for MM. This means that there exists a number a0a_{0} such that paE​(M)=1p_{a}^{E}(M)=1 for all a≥a0a\geq a_{0}.
Remark 1.1.
Let (M4,ω)(M^{4},\omega) be a compact, connected symplectic 44-manifold with smooth boundary. Let a0a_{0} denote the threshold from Theorem B. Fix a>a0a>a_{0} and consider the symplectic ellipsoid E=E⁡(r,r​a)E=E(r,ra) where the parameter r>0r>0 is chosen so that vol⁡(M)=vol⁡(E)\operatorname{vol}(M)=\operatorname{vol}(E). This means that the closed symplectic ellipsoid λ​E\lambda E symplectically embeds into the interior of MM for all λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1). This naturally raises the question of whether the interior of EE itself admits a symplectic embedding into the interior of MM. In light of [PV15, Theorem 4.4], this would follow if one could arrange the symplectic embeddings of λ​E\lambda E into the interior of MM to depend smoothly on λ\lambda as λ\lambda approaches 11. It is conceivable that, with additional care, such a smooth dependence can be achieved using the symplectic embedding constructions developed in this paper. However, we will not pursue this direction further here and leave it for future work.
In the literature, the ellipsoid embedding numbers paE​(M)p_{a}^{E}(M) of a symplectic 44-manifold (M,ω)(M,\omega) are often encoded in terms of the ellipsoid embedding function cM:[0,∞)→ℝc_{M}:[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}; see, for example, [CHMP25]. This function is defined by
cM​(a)≔inf{r∣E⁡(1,a)​↪𝑠​(M,r​ω)},c_{M}(a)\coloneqq\inf\left\{r\mid E(1,a)\overset{s}{\hookrightarrow}(M,r\omega)\right\},
where X​↪𝑠​YX\overset{s}{\hookrightarrow}Y denotes the existence of a symplectic embedding from XX into YY. The function cM​(a)c_{M}(a) encodes the same information as the ellipsoid embedding numbers paE​(M)p_{a}^{E}(M).
The ellipsoid embedding function cMc_{M} is notoriously difficult to compute. In a landmark paper, McDuff and Schlenk [MS12] succeeded in computing the ellipsoid embedding function cB⁡(1)c_{B(1)} of the 44-dimensional ball—arguably the simplest nontrivial target manifold. Their result is an intricate yet explicit function featuring the so-called infinite Fibonacci staircase. A further key feature of cB⁡(1)c_{B(1)} is that for sufficiently large aa, the function stabilizes to the volume curve:
cB⁡(1)​(a)=a2​vol⁡(B⁡(1))=a.c_{B(1)}(a)=\sqrt{\frac{a}{2\operatorname{vol}(B(1))}}=\sqrt{a}.
This stabilization is equivalent to the assertion that ellipsoid embedding stability holds for B⁡(1)B(1).
For a general compact, connected symplectic 44-manifold MM with smooth boundary, fully computing the function cMc_{M} appears entirely out of reach. Nevertheless, Theorem B shows that cMc_{M} always stabilizes to the volume curve.
1.3. Limits of packing stability
As mentioned above, Cristofaro-Gardiner and Hind [CHa] constructed the first examples of symplectic manifolds of finite volume that do not exhibit ball packing stability. For a discussion of the failure of packing stability in the context of packings by certain generalized convex toric domains, rather than by balls, we refer the reader to [CMM].

1 Introduction
In [Bir97, Bir99], Biran discovered the packing stability phenomenon: in some symplectic 44-manifolds, the symplectic obstructions to pack NN identical balls disappear when NN becomes large enough. He later generalized this result to every closed symplectic 44-manifold with rational symplectic class ([ω]∈H2​(M,ℚ)[\omega]\in H^{2}(M,\mathbb{Q})).
In this paper we generalize these results in several directions, by applying the singular inflation technique developed in [Ops13b, MO13]. We generalize Biran’s packing stability to all symplectic 44-manifolds, and also to a class of open symplectic 44-manifolds including ellipsoids and domains we call pseudo-balls.
For these manifolds, we establish not just packing stability but strong packing stability, which we define now. The definition is in the spirit of Biran’s first results on the subject [Bir97]. Throughout B⁡(λ)B(\lambda) will denote an open ball of capacity λ\lambda (see Definition 1.3) and we will write U​↪𝜔​VU\overset{\omega}{\hookrightarrow}V for a symplectic embedding.
Definition 1.1.
A symplectic manifold XX has property 𝒫⁡(λ)\mathcal{P}(\lambda) if for all collection of real numbers (λi)(\lambda_{i}) with λi<λ​∀i\lambda_{i}<\lambda\;\forall i, ⊔B⁡(λi)​↪𝜔​X\sqcup B(\lambda_{i})\overset{\omega}{\hookrightarrow}X if and only if the volume obstruction 12​∑λi2≤Vol⁡(X)\frac{1}{2}\sum\lambda_{i}^{2}\leq\mathrm{Vol}(X) is satisfied. We say that XX has the strong packing stability if it satisfies 𝒫⁡(λ)\mathcal{P}(\lambda) for some λ\lambda. We then define
Λ⁡(X):=inf{λ|X​ verifies ​𝒫​(λ)}.\Lambda(X):=\inf\{\lambda\;|\;X\text{ verifies }\mathcal{P}(\lambda)\}.
If there exists a μ\mu such that for all λ<μ\lambda<\mu we have ⊔B⁡(λ)​↪𝜔​X\sqcup B(\lambda)\overset{\omega}{\hookrightarrow}X if and only if the volume obstruction is satisfied, then we say that XX has packing stability. (In other words, we only consider embeddings by equally sized balls.)
Remark 1.2.
Since the volume inequality used is not strict, this definition even of packing stability is stronger than those used previously (for example in [BH11]) which ask for embeddings only if the union of balls has strictly smaller volume. Of course, to obtain embeddings in the case of equal volume, it is necessary for us to work with open balls. Such embeddings were called very full fillings in [LMS12], section 77.
Our main result is the following.
Theorem 1.
All closed 44-dimensional symplectic manifolds have strong packing stability.
To prove this theorem we will first need to establish strong packing stability for some open symplectic manifolds, and these results are interesting in themselves. To define these domains we work in ℂ2\mathbb{C}^{2} with its standard symplectic form.
Definition 1.3.
Let U⊂ℂ2U\subset\mathbb{C}^{2} be the interior of a domain of the form {(z,w)∈ℂ2|(π​|z|2,π​|w|2)∈P}\{(z,w)\in\mathbb{C}^{2}\;|\;(\pi|z|^{2},\pi|w|^{2})\in P\} where PP is a subset of the first quadrant in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}.
If PP is the convex hull P=Conv​⟨(0,0),(a,0),(0,b)⟩P=\text{Conv}\,\langle(0,0),(a,0),(0,b)\rangle then we say UU is a symplectic ellipsoid E⁡(a,b)E(a,b). A ball of capacity aa is an ellipsoid B⁡(a)=E⁡(a,a)B(a)=E(a,a), and we write τ​E​(a,b)\tau E(a,b) for E⁡(τ​a,τ​b)E(\tau a,\tau b).
If P=Conv​⟨(0,0),(0,a),(b,0),(α,β)⟩P=\text{Conv}\,\langle(0,0),(0,a),(b,0),(\alpha,\beta)\rangle for some a>αa>\alpha, b>βb>\beta and a,b<α+βa,b<\alpha+\beta then we say that UU is a pseudo-ball T⁡(a,b,α,β)T(a,b,\alpha,\beta).
Now we can state the following.
Theorem 2.
The 44-dimensional ellipsoids have the strong packing stability. Moreover, the function Λ⁡(E⁡(1,a))\Lambda(E(1,a)) is locally bounded on ℝ∗\mathbb{R}^{*}.
Note that since any rational symplectic manifold has full packing by an ellipsoid [Ops07], this theorem clearly implies Biran’s original result.
Corollary 1.4.
All closed symplectic 44-manifolds with rational symplectic class have the packing stability.
Strong packing stability for ellipsoids does not immediately imply packing stability for all closed manifolds, however, because the following remains a conjecture.
Conjecture 1.
Every (closed) 44-dimensional symplectic manifold is fully packed by one ellipsoid.
Nevertheless we will show that any symplectic 44 manifold can be decomposed (up to a subset of volume 00) into finitely many open symplectic manifolds, each of which has a Hamiltonian toric free action with convex associated polytope, namely ellipsoids and pseudo-balls. Theorem 1 will then follow from Theorem 2 and the following strong packing stability for pseudo-balls.
Theorem 3.
The pseudo-balls have the strong packing stability. Moreover, the function Λ⁡(T⁡(a,b,α,β))\Lambda(T(a,b,\alpha,\beta)) is locally bounded on {α<a<α+β,β<b<α+β}⊂ℝ4\{\alpha<a<\alpha+\beta,\beta<b<\alpha+\beta\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{4}.
Related results.
In [BH11, BH13], the first two authors proved that rational symplectic manifolds in all dimensions have packing stability. It remains an open question whether higher dimensional rational manifolds have strong packing stability. The proof argued as in Corollary 1.4 by first showing that all ellipsoids have packing stability and then remarking that any rational symplectic manifold admits a volume filling embedding from an ellipsoid. The ellipsoid packing stability ultimately relied on an embedding result for 44-dimensional ellipsoids.
Theorem.
[Buse-Hind] There exists a continuous function f:[1,∞)→[1,∞)f:[1,\infty)\to[1,\infty) such that if b>f⁡(a)b>f(a) then there exists a symplectic embedding λ​E​(1,b)→E⁡(1,a)\lambda E(1,b)\to E(1,a) if any only if the volume condition is satisfied.
This immediately implies ellipsoid packing stability in four dimensions since an ellipsoid E⁡(1,k)E(1,k) can be fully filled by kk balls. The proof of the above theorem in [BH13] relied on Embedded Contact Homology, although the theorem in fact also follows from the strong packing stability we establish here. Indeed, work of McDuff says that an ellipsoid embedding in dimension 44 exists whenever there exists an embedding of a union of balls of appropriate sizes. It would be interesting to compare the corresponding bounds on the function ff.
Recent work of Latschev, McDuff and Schlenk in [LMS12] implies packing stability of 44-dimensional tori with linear symplectic forms (most of which are irrational). Indeed, if TT is a linear 44-dimensional torus not a product of 22-dimensional tori of equal area then we have an embedding ⊔B⁡(λi)​↪𝜔​X\sqcup B(\lambda_{i})\overset{\omega}{\hookrightarrow}X whenever the volume obstruction 12​∑λi2<Vol⁡(X)\frac{1}{2}\sum\lambda_{i}^{2}<\mathrm{Vol}(X) is satisfied. For the product T⁡(μ,μ)T(\mu,\mu) of two tori of area μ\mu this remains true given the additional condition that λi<μ\lambda_{i}<\mu for all ii. However whether or not there exist very full fillings of tori under just these hypotheses remains an open question.
Organization of the paper and description of methods.
As mentioned
above,
the main ingredient for our arguments is to show that two types of open symplectic manifolds, an ellipsoid and a pseudo-ball,
have strong packing stability. The conclusion of the proof of packing stability for ellipsoids (Theorem 2) is found in section 3.3 and explain how the case of the pseudo-ball (Theorem 3) follows along the same lines in section 4.
Both these results are consequences of two technical lemmas, which we deal with first. One is a basic result on packing stability of blow-ups of ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2},
proved in section 2,
which serves as a building block for all our other packing stability results.
Lemma 1.5.
All symplectic forms on the pp-fold blow-up ℙ^p2\hat{\mathbb{P}}^{2}_{p} of ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} have the strong packing stability. Moreover Λ⁡(ω^)\Lambda(\hat{\omega}) is bounded from below by a quantity which depends only on the volume of (ℙp2,ω^)(\mathbb{P}^{2}_{p},\hat{\omega}).
